posts.name: Zack Weinberg
posts.cooked:
I am writing a client library for a bespoke local RPC protocol. The service implementation is not under my control, so I can't change the protocol. Inconveniently, the protocol packet format embeds libc::sockaddr_* structs directly in each message; the message format looks something like this

#[repr(C)]
union PacketAddr {
    sin: libc::sockaddr_in,
    sin6: libc::sockaddr_in6,
    ss: libc::sockaddr_storage,
}

#[repr(C)]
struct Packet {
    packet_len: u32,
    proto_ver: u32,
    msg_type: u32,
    addr_len: u32, 
    addr: PacketAddr,
    annotation: [u8],
};

(The addr_len field tells you which field of the PacketAddr union is live but does not control where annotation starts; addr is always the full size of the union, zero-padded internally if necessary. annotation runs from that point to the end of the packet as defined by packet_len.)

Now, in order to talk this protocol over a local communication channel, one must somehow go from the above struct definition to a &[u8] that can be passed to libc::send. The problem is, the fields of sockaddr_* are not fully pinned down by any standard and in practice do vary between Unixes (N.B. this software is never going to support Windows), so I cannot copy addresses (along with the rest of the packet) field by field into a Cursor<Vec<u8>>, which is what I would usually do.

zerocopy's IntoBytes trait would be just the ticket, but I cannot use it because of the orphan rule (I'm not allowed to #[derive(IntoBytes)] for sockaddr_in because neither of those is defined by my crate).

Instead I came up with this hack:

/// Coerce an arbitrary type S (presumably some kind of struct sockaddr_XX)
/// to a &[u8] slice covering its bytes.
unsafe fn sockaddr_as_bytes<S>(sa: &S) -> &[u8] {
    // SAFETY: This fabricates an &[u8] slice that covers `sa`
    // exactly.  Each byte of the slice is valid for read because `sa`
    // itself was valid for read.  &[u8] cannot be misaligned and u8
    // has no invalid states.  Caller is responsible for ensuring S
    // has a fixed layout and `sa` is fully initialized including padding.
    unsafe {
        slice::from_raw_parts(sa as *const S as *const u8, mem::size_of::<S>())
    }
}

... which is basically what zerocopy's IntoBytes would do for me, but with fewer safety rails. It works, but I don't feel particularly good about it.

So the questions I have are:

  1. Is there a more "official" way to do the above? That is, did I miss something in std::mem or std::ptr that encapsulates at least some of the unsafety?
  2. Is there a way to subvert the orphan rule so I can use zerocopy? Or is there some other third-party crate that would be helpful?
  3. Supposing I'm stuck with the unsafe hack, is my understanding of what needs to be true for the function to be OK to use (as encapsulated by the safety comment) accurate? Did I miss anything important?

creating a slice reference &[u8] to padding bytes is UB, unless you wrap it in MaybeUninit, such as &[MaybeUninit<u8>].

alternatively, you can use a raw pointer *const u8 plus the length, instead of slice reference &[u8]. raw pointers doesn't have the validity requirement, and is ok to be passed to ffi functions such as libc::send(), but make sure you don't dereference the raw pointer in rust.

for this particular use case,

What about manually adding padding, like

const PADDED_LEN: usize = /* maximum of the three sizes */;

#[repr(C)]
struct PaddedSockAddrIn {
    pub data: libc::sockaddr_in,
    pub padding: [u8; { PADDED_LEN - size_of::<libc::sockaddr_in>() }],
}

// and so on

Then, assuming the libc::sockaddr_* types consist entirely of plain-old-bytes (no uninit or pointers), one could fearlessly use mem::transmute<PacketAddr, [u8: PADDED_LEN]>(_) (or cast the references, or whatever) as both the input and output type would have no safety or validity invariants beyond being PADDED_LEN-many pointer-provenance-free initialized bytes.

For 3: “u8 has no invalid states” is false. Bytes in Rust’s Abstract Machine look something like

enum AbstractByte {
    Uninit,
    Init(u8, Option<PointerProvenance>),
}

and valid states (more precisely, valid “representations”) of u8s are abstract bytes matching AbstractByte::Init(_, None).

Would the following not work and be a touch safer?

  1. Vec with capacity packet_len
  2. push 1st 4 fields
  3. unsafe slice from raw parts addr & copy into Vec
  4. unsafe slice from raw parts annotation & copy into Vec

posts.name: Kevin Reid
posts.cooked:
zackw:

That's the issue I was trying to cover with "Caller is responsible for ensuring ... sa is fully initialized including padding". ... But I am 100% stuck with "the format of this field is whatever libc::sockaddr_in{,6} is on this target", so "better ideas" somehow have to involve knowing all the fields of those structures.

In Rust, the only way to know that memory for a struct is initialized including the padding between the fields is to write all fields individually at their correct offset (in addition to initializing the padding, perhaps by starting with zeroed memory). Every write operation that uses the struct type as a whole is allowed to write uninit to padding areas, even if it's a move from a location where the padding was initialized. So, you cannot do this without knowing field offsets or knowing there is no padding.

Given the hard constraints -- I cannot change the packet format, I need to copy the native-endian bytes of every field (standardized or not) of a sockaddr_in[6] to the appropriate location within a larger &mut [u8], and zero all the bytes that were padding in the source, and the set of fields and their offsets is OS-dependent -- how would you proceed?

I think you will need to know which bytes are padding and which ones are not. If you do know that then you can first copy the struct into a MaybeUninit buffer, then zero the padding and then copy it into the output.

If you did not care about the value of the padding bytes on the wire you could have used something like the probably coming freeze operation, but if they need to be zero, i don't think this would help at all.

Please understand that this is the part I need help with.

Just to illustrate the problem, this is the definition of struct sockaddr_in from the Linux kernel's UAPI headers (after erasing a bunch of macro gunk and replacing typedefs with their definitions):

struct in_addr {
    unsigned int s_addr;
};
struct sockaddr_in {
    unsigned short  sin_family;
    unsigned short  sin_port;
    struct in_addr  sin_addr;
    unsigned char   sin_zero[
      16 - (sizeof(unsigned short)
            + sizeof(unsigned short)
            + sizeof(struct in_addr))
    ];
};

And this is the definition from NetBSD:

struct in_addr {
    unsigned int    s_addr;
};
struct sockaddr_in {
    unsigned char   sin_len;
    unsigned char   sin_family;
    unsigned short  sin_port;
    struct in_addr  sin_addr;
    signed char     sin_zero[8];
};

Notice how even the fields common to all sockaddr structures are not the same between the two clades.

posts.name: Zack Weinberg
posts.cooked: I can guarantee a deterministic layout, but not no padding, and more importantly, I can't guarantee a target-independent layout. If the layout were target-independent I could just copy all of the fields to the right locations and be done.

zackw:

Ugh. The most common implementations should avoid having any padding but I do not know that for sure. I feel like "allowed to write uninit to padding areas even if..." is a bad rule in general

I believe there are at least two reasons for this:

  • Being able to pass the struct fields one by one in registers rather than on the stack.
  • It might be cheaper (or required) on some architectures to write whole aligned words, so any smaller unit means reading a word in, modifying it and writing it back. Being able to ignore padding allows optimising away such reads sometimes.

I'm going to leave out the discussions about if those optimisations are worth it or not.

@farnz is correct: I'm writing a client library for a service I didn't design. I start with a Rust-native SocketAddrV4 (or V6) and I need to turn that into the native byte serialization of a C sockaddr_in (or _in6), which will be embedded in the larger packet as shown and sent off to the service. It's a completely fire-and-forget protocol, the server never replies to anything, so I only need to encode packets. And it doesn't make sense to run this particular service on a different host from its clients, so the C sockaddr_in will always line up between server and client ... unless we get some virtual machines involved, I suppose, but I don't think the service's authors were thinking about that at all.

(I probably am going to end up writing my own server implementation eventually, but that is not today's problem.)

So, XY is a fair question, but I really don't see an alternative. I would not have designed this protocol this way, but I don't get to change it.

I'm not ready to share my crate publicly, but the service is NetBSD's blocklistd, and if you would like to see the C protocol implementation, it can be found here: bl.c. And the reason I'm writing my own client is because there are several things about the bl.c client implementation that make it unpleasant to call via FFI from Rust. It seems to have been designed with "we want to patch existing network daemons to use this, but we have no plans to upstream those patches so we need them to be minimally invasive so we can carry them indefinitely" as a top-priority design goal.

Vorpal:

... sticking entirely to MaybeUninit or raw pointers is the way to go ...

I don't think either MaybeUninit or raw pointers will actually help, because I need the entire packet to be fully initialized by the time I feed it to send. If I used a copy method that copied uninitialized bytes safely, I would then need to find those uninitialized bytes (if any) and initialize them. Which reduces to the same problem of needing to know which bytes are padding.

My current vague plan is to have a module with a bunch of #[cfg()] conditionals that knows how to build up a sockaddr_in(6) field by field, and then use bindgen to generate a test that validates what that module knows, thus avoiding having the crate proper depend on bindgen.

Given that both of those definitions from Linux and NetBSD have no padding (assuming that an int is at most twice the size of a short which is at most twice the size of a char, and likewise for their alignments, as should be the case in sane C environments), is the problem that you can’t guarantee there’s no padding on every OS?

If you’re considering using cfg to initialize field-by-field… perhaps it would be better to use cfg to enforce that only targets with known-sane definitions of the packet structs are supported.

posts.name: Simon Farnsworth
posts.cooked:
Given that this is effectively an FFI boundary, maybe make use of the fact that reading padding bytes is defined in C as returning an arbitrary byte value that can change on every read?

Something along the lines of (rigorously untested and may not compile):

fn packet_addr_to_byte_array(pa: PacketAddr) -> [u8; std::mem::size_of::<PacketAddr>] {
    let mut out = [0u8; std::mem::size_of::<PacketAddr>];
    // SAFETY: Destination allocated above, so guaranteed large enough
    unsafe { libc::memcpy(&mut out, &pa, std::mem::size_of::<PacketAddr>()); }
}

This way, you're doing what the C code would do, which is defined behaviour in C, and has a Rust story making it legal to do via FFI (you're reading the bytes of PacketAddr, replacing the padding with arbitrary values).

Memcpy is special though, and both LLVM and Miri knows it. This came up on zulip a few weeks ago. So it will copy the uninit bytes rather than turn them into arbitrary values. What you actually need is to do this in inline assembly so it is entirely opaque to the compiler.

farnz:

This way, you're doing what the C code would do, which is defined behaviour in C, and has a Rust story making it legal to do via FFI (you're reading the bytes of PacketAddr, replacing the padding with arbitrary values).

That isn't a story, is it?

Anyway, I'd rely on the proposition that system APIs don't accept uninit and thus libc::sockaddr_* doesn't have internal padding. As for code, it would copy addr_len bytes of the address into the outgoing buffer and then zero-pad it by hand.

posts.name: Simon Farnsworth
posts.cooked:
Vorpal:

Memcpy is special though, and both LLVM and Miri knows it. This came up on zulip a few weeks ago. So it will copy the uninit bytes rather than turn them into arbitrary values. What you actually need is to do this in inline assembly so it is entirely opaque to the compiler.

That's why I'm using libc::memcpy, which, being a C memcpy, has to meet C's rules for copying, not Rust's (substituting std::ptr::copy, which is also a memcpy, would be wrong because it meets Rust's rules for memcpy, not C's rules).

In turn, while memcpy may well be special to LLVM, it's a bug in Miri if it assumes that a C memcpy copying a #[repr(C)] struct, behaves like Rust code, not C code.

Otherwise, your assertion is that I can take fully defined C code that copies padding with memcpy, link it via FFI with Rust, and cause the C code to develop UB because it meets Rust's rules, not C's rules - that feels like a big reach to me. LLVM has to at least understand that C memcpy meets C's rules, and therefore should account for that in the LLVM implementation (by using freeze or equivalent semantics).

ProgramCrafter:

That isn't a story, is it?

I don't see why not - I'm explaining what the Rust AM would do if it were copying the FFI code's behaviour - it would copy the entire union, replacing padding by arbitrary byte values that can change each time I call this function. That's a story about what Rust code would do if it knew the full layout of all the members of the union, and is therefore good enough.

One potential (somewhat hacky) approach is to pin version (using version="=x.y.z" in your Cargo.toml) of the crate which defines the struct and write unsafe code using knowledge of the exact struct definition (such as lack of padding bytes). But ideally you should reach the library authors and ask them to implement IntoBytes where appropriate.

First: you are assuming no cross language LTO here. Second, even in the C AM memcpy copies and preserves uninit bytes as uninit as far as I understand. And yes, rust and llvm both make assumptions about what exactly the unmangled symbol memcpy is. See also core - Rust for a few more symbols Rust make assumptions about.

posts.name: Simon Farnsworth
posts.cooked:
If cross-language LTO changes the defined behaviour of the C code to UB, then there is a bug in LLVM. It is simply wrong to optimize code with defined behaviour such that it now has undefined behaviour, regardless of whether that's cross-language LTO or not.

And yes, both Rust and LLVM make assumptions about what the unmangled symbol memcpy does, which is why I can't simply use std::ptr::copy (which is defined as using memcpy within the Rust AM). But I should be able to use libc::memcpy within the C AM to get the C AM behaviour where the bytes are frozen on copy, as long as the object's address is taken.

Target-dependence is not a problem as long as you fetch the target size & alignment.

farnz:

what Rust code would do if it knew the full layout of all the members of the union

"To know the full layout of a type" is not expressible in Rust code, and that is the problem.

Replacing uninitialized bytes with arbitrary init bytes is freeze operation and it is not introduced yet; Rust AM does not define[1] any operation that works like that.

I looked more into sockaddr_* structures and their POSIX requirements and how they are passed (most importantly, into kernel); they are passed by pointer, so nothing stops them from having padding inside in principle. But if it had, blocklistd would probably be unsound too, so it doesn't matter.

Conclusion: make a zeroed vector and copy addr_len bytes there.

  1. similarity to words "undefined behavior" fully intended ↩︎

Again, it's a miscompilation if C code called by Rust has to meet the rules of the Rust AM - if you're saying that any C code linked by Rust has to meet the rules of the Rust AM, not the C AM, then all C FFI is unsound by definition.

Are you familiar with Ralf Jung’s blog post on “storytelling”? Inline asm and FFI aren’t permitted to do anything to the AM that no Rust code could do. (The code could also do other stuff outside the AM, but the C code’s effects on the Rust AM are bound by the rules of the Rust AM. It might also do weird things in intermediate states, if it’s provable that nothing in the Rust AM could observe the temporary weirdness.)

posts.name: Simon Farnsworth
posts.cooked:
I am - but the Rust code I'm envisioning knows the type and layout of libc::sockaddr_in etc, and is able to use offset_of! and size_of to only read valid bytes, and where there's padding in libc::sockadd_in etc, it will write some arbitrary byte value, possibly chosen via rand::thread_rng.

The story is thus one that Rust code could implement - it's just that the Rust code in question is highly tied to the definition of the type, and therefore a pain to implement. I'm not talking about something that cannot be implemented in the Rust AM, which would not qualify as a story.

The blog post emphasizes that this is "as far as the state observable by pure Rust code is concerned". The stack painting example explicitly states

An alternative story is to say that the asm block just returns some arbitrary, non-deterministically chosen value

with the qualification that

when reasoning about our code, we cannot make any assumptions about the value we read

which is totally fine by use because we do not care about the value of the padding bytes. The important part is that the non-padding bytes are those from the initial struct. So we chose the story for an inline assembly block to copy the initialized bytes and write arbitrary, non-deterministic values for the padding bytes.

As Ralf writes in footnote 1, cross-language LTO might put additional restrictions on us, so the question is, can we use the same story for a libc::memcpy invocation and get away with it. As far as I understand, farnz argues that it is a bug in the LTO if it is not allowed.

I do not have a reference for this to hand, but I distinctly remember reading about 10 years ago that there is a dispute regarding whether, in C, memcpy can soundly be applied to partially initialized memory. (In other words, the thing that some people are insisting is totally fine in the C abstract machine might not actually be allowed. Yes, lots of C programs, including the one I'm wrestling with, do it anyway. Soundness hasn't historically been a primary concern for C programmers )

posts.name: Simon Farnsworth
posts.cooked:
zackw:

I do not have a reference for this to hand, but I distinctly remember reading about 10 years ago that there is a dispute regarding whether, in C, memcpy can soundly be applied to partially initialized memory. (In other words, the thing that some people are insisting is totally fine in the C abstract machine might not actually be allowed. Yes, lots of C programs, including the one I'm wrestling with, do it anyway. Soundness hasn't historically been a primary concern for C programmers )

In C11 specifically, it's governed by the rules in 6.2.6.1, paragraph 6:

When a value is stored in an object of structure or union type, including in a member
object, the bytes of the object representation that correspond to any padding bytes take
unspecified values. The value of a structure or union object is never a trap
representation, even though the value of a member of the structure or union object may be
a trap representation.

Paragraph 5 defines when trap representations are expected - notably, if you're accessing other than through the type or a character type (memcpy is defined as accessing through a character type), you can face trap representations, which are not safe to copy.

So, it's not safe to access the sockaddr_in member of your union if someone has written a sockaddr_in6 to it (this is UB in C, but interestingly, only UB in Rust if std::mem::size_of<sockaddr_in>() > std::mem::size_of<sockaddr_in6>() - Rust doesn't track active member for this purpose, unlike C and C++). It is always safe in C to memcpy from the union, or to cast to a character type (e.g. char *) and read it that way - it's just that the padding bytes are unspecified value, and in C, that permits (but does not require) the padding bytes to read differently on every read.

This also means that casting to uint32_t * to let you do the copy "faster" is UB in the C AM, unless uint32_t on your compiler is defined as a character type - only char, unsigned char and signed char are defined as character types by the Standard. memcpy, while it takes void * is defined as doing the accesses through a character type, which makes it legal to memcpy.

zackw:

Interesting suggestion, but I said the above before I realized that it may be system-dependent whether #[derive(IntoBytes)] would actually go through on these types. So, in the zerocopy maintainers' shoes, I'd be hesitant to accept the PR.

At the risk of feature creep, it sounds like something along the lines of a fallible TryIntoBytes trait might be useful here, where the impl for a given type can be made platform-dependent using cargo features, or the family of cfg macros.
